subject: maths

moments.title: Galois at school in Paris
moments.body:
Galois discovers mathematics at age 14 and tears through it: Lagrange, Gauss, Cauchy. At 17 he proves that no general formula (in radicals) exists for solving polynomials of degree 5 or higher. The result had been claimed by Ruffini (1799) and proved rigorously by Abel (1824). Galois proves it AND gives a complete criterion for when a polynomial is solvable.

He submits his work to the Paris Academy. Cauchy mishandles the manuscript (later lost). Fourier dies before reading a second submission. Poisson finds a third version incomprehensible and rejects it.
moments.takeaway: Galois invents what we now call group theory. His papers are rejected, lost or misunderstood by the establishment.

moments.title: Galois in revolution
moments.body:
Galois becomes an active republican during the July Revolution. He attends meetings, threatens to assassinate the king at a banquet, and is arrested twice. He spends most of 1831 in prison.

Released in spring 1832, he becomes embroiled in a duel — possibly over a woman, possibly engineered by political enemies, possibly both. Knowing he may die, he stays up the night of 29 May writing out his mathematical results in detail.

On the morning of 30 May 1832, he is shot in the stomach. He dies the next day. He is 20 years old.

quote.text: Please, Alfred, do not weep — I need all my courage to die at 20.
quote.attrib: Galois to his younger brother, on his deathbed

moments.takeaway: Most of what Galois knew about mathematics dies with him. His last-night notes are all that survives.

moments.title: Liouville recovers Galois's papers
moments.body:
Galois's brother Alfred and his friend Alfred Chevalier preserve his papers and try for years to get them published. Liouville finally edits and publishes them in 1846, 14 years after Galois's death.

The papers transform algebra. Liouville's introduction calls Galois's results 'as profound as they are subtle'.
moments.takeaway: It took 14 years for Galois's work to reach the mathematical community.

moments.title: Group theory established
moments.body:
Arthur Cayley defines abstract groups (1854). Camille Jordan publishes the first textbook on group theory in 1870, dedicated to Galois. Sylow's theorems (1872) give structural results. Group theory becomes a central pillar of abstract algebra and, later, physics.

Without the language of groups, the symmetry foundations of quantum mechanics, particle physics and general relativity would have been impossible.
moments.takeaway: Galois's 18-year-old's insight becomes the foundational language of symmetry in mathematics and physics.

now.title: Group theory today
now.body:
Groups describe symmetries of everything: crystals, atoms, fundamental forces, error-correcting codes, cryptographic systems, knot invariants. The classification of finite simple groups (completed 2004) is one of the largest single results in mathematical history — over 10,000 pages by hundreds of authors.

Lie groups generalise to continuous symmetries and are central to gauge theories in physics.
now.open_questions: Are there finite simple groups we haven't classified? (Probably not — but verification of the proof is ongoing.) Can we generalise group theory to deeper algebraic structures? Why do Lie groups (specifically SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1)) describe the fundamental forces?

reflection: Galois worked out an entirely new branch of mathematics before he turned 21 and died before anyone could understand it. What is the cost of brilliance dying young? How much of mathematics history depends on the survival of people who don't get killed in revolutions and duels?
